candidates.headline: Midjourney's new anime model, Niji 8, is live and can put the same character into new scenes
candidates.what_happened: Midjourney and Spellbrush released Niji 8, their anime and illustration image model, on 24 November 2026. It adds an edit feature that poses a character from one picture into another background, the replacement for the character reference tool many users missed. Plans start at $10 a month, or $8 a month billed yearly; there is no free plan on the pricing page.

primary.label: niji・journey blog, Welcome to Niji 8, 24 Nov 2026
primary.quote: Many of you missed the cref feature from Niji 6. After much work, we’re finally back with its replacement: the edit feature, which allows you to pose your characters into different backgrounds while keeping consistency.

second.label: Midjourney on X, 24 Nov 2026
second.quote: This is our latest anime model with precision prompting, consistent characters, best in class coherence, a dedicated editing model and more.

more_sources.label: niji・journey pricing page
more_sources.quote: Basic Plan Regular price $10 With yearly billing $8 / month 20% off billed annually

steps.text: Pick Niji 8 from the Version menu in the settings beside the prompt bar on the web, or add --niji 8 after your prompt in Discord.
Keep prompts short when you want a spread of ideas; write longer prompts when you know what you want, because Niji 8 reads length as intent.
To keep one character across scenes, press the quick edit button at the bottom right of a finished image and attach a character sheet and a background.
Prompt with two pictures, such as take the character from image 1 and put it into image 2, and use sharp, unpixelated inputs for the best result.
A plan is needed: Basic is $10 a month, or $8 a month billed yearly.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: Character consistency moves from typing the same words (Niji 7) to an image edit model, so an illustrator can lock a character from a reference sheet and still get variety from short prompts.
candidates.why_it_matters: Comic, storyboard and animation makers can now keep one character on model across panels inside a $10 a month tool.
candidates.funny: The release note admits the developers lost their own favourite test character when the new model changed how prompts behave.
candidates.risks: Company page only, plus its own X post; no independent review yet. Midjourney's docs site refused to load (403), so plan details come from the nijijourney pricing page.

candidates.headline: The New York Times told its freelance photographers not to use the new Photoshop
candidates.what_happened: In an email reported by The Verge on 24 November 2026, two New York Times photography leaders told freelancers to avoid Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and later) on assignment. They said its AI features can add metadata that labels a photograph as AI-generated, which a newsroom that does not retouch photos cannot risk. A Times spokesperson confirmed the requirement.

primary.label: The Verge, The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features, 24 Nov 2026
primary.quote: “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads.

second.label: Peter Baker on Threads, posting the email, about 24 Nov 2026
second.quote: Using Photoshop is an occupational hazard now. NY Times banning photographers from using the latest version.

more_sources.label: The Verge, same article
more_sources.quote: The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.”

candidates.money_or_mechanism: Adobe's content credentials tag any AI-touched edit, so one routine tool can mark a news photo as AI-edited and cost the paper reader trust, while the freelancer risks the commission.
candidates.why_it_matters: A photographer's software update can now decide whether a client will accept the pictures.
candidates.funny: The world's best-known newspaper is asking photographers to keep their software out of date on purpose.
candidates.risks: The email itself was seen by The Verge and posted on Threads; the Threads page showed the post text but not the email image. Adobe had not responded. Adobe's release notes page refused to load (403). Not clear which exact features trigger the label.

candidates.headline: Musicians are using AI to rewrite their synths' software, and makers are opening up their code
candidates.what_happened: The Verge reported on 25 November 2026 that AI coding tools have let hobbyists write custom firmware for music gear, and that companies are responding by open-sourcing devices. M-Vave's $70 FM-1 now has well over a dozen custom firmwares; inMusic, owner of Akai, Moog and Native Instruments, has released an SDK; Polyend published its Tracker firmware code. Elektron has banned links to custom firmware from its forums.
candidates.named_thing: M-Vave FM-1, the $70 synth with over a dozen AI-era custom firmwares

primary.label: The Verge, Has vibe coding made open source the new normal for synths?, 25 Nov 2026
primary.quote: In the last several weeks, as it’s become clear that no piece of music gear is safe from Claude and a subreddit full of curious tinkerers, companies have begun making more and more of their devices open source.

second.label: Polyend, Tracker. The biggest update yet, 2 Nov 2026
second.quote: Today we’re publishing the firmware source code for the original Tracker, Tracker+ and Tracker Mini on GitHub.

more_sources.label: The Verge, same article, inMusic chief executive Jack O'Donnell
more_sources.quote: “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want,” inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell tells The Verge.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: When anyone can rewrite a box's firmware with an AI agent, a cheap synth gains features its maker never sold, and makers choose between opening the code or fighting warranty claims.
candidates.why_it_matters: A producer can get new life from gear they already own instead of buying the next box.
candidates.funny: A $70 clone of a 1980s Yamaha became the synth of the summer because people kept teaching it new tricks with chatbots.
candidates.risks: Feature piece built on interviews; the Polyend source is dated 2 November, before the window. Modding can void warranties or brick gear (Elektron's warning), so any steps must carry that caveat.

candidates.headline: Etsy rewrote its AI training terms after sellers revolted, and many say they will still leave
candidates.what_happened: Etsy changed its terms of use to let it train AI models on sellers' listings, and after a backlash posted clarified terms on Monday 23 November 2026, The Verge reported on 25 November. Chief executive Kruti Patel Goyal wrote that Etsy will not use sellers' content to make copycat versions of their work, but many sellers still plan to leave.
candidates.named_thing: Etsy's revised terms of use on AI training

primary.label: The Verge, Etsy clarified its AI training policy, but sellers still aren’t happy, 25 Nov 2026
primary.quote: “We will not use your content to create copycat versions of the work you sell on Etsy. We use your content to build tools that do things like help buyers find your items, help you run your shop, improve customer support, promote your work, and keep our marketplace safe.”

second.label: The Verge, Etsy says it will revise its new AI policy after backlash from sellers, 20 Nov 2026
second.quote: Earlier this week, Ossman said in an update on Etsy’s new terms of use, “We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity. Again, this is not changing.”

candidates.money_or_mechanism: Sellers' photos and descriptions are the training data for Etsy's own search and shop tools; the dispute is whether makers are paid, or can opt out, when their work trains them.
candidates.why_it_matters: Craft and design sellers are learning that the marketplace they pay fees to can also train AI on their listings.
candidates.funny: The company had to promise in writing that its AI will not copy the handmade things it exists to sell.
candidates.risks: Both sources are The Verge (two separate posts), which cites the CEO's blog and the New York Times; Etsy's own pages refused to load (403), so the CEO quote is as quoted by The Verge. No real image of the thing itself found; the media link is a placeholder and should be replaced. Sits close to policy; keep it on who gets paid for the work.
